User: I need help with my 2023 tax return. I'm head of household in Chicago IL. My W-2 from TechStart Inc shows $64,800. I had $15,000 in 1099 income (marketing, 2 clients), $1,450 from Goldman Sachs Marcus, and $320 from TD Ameritrade. I have a home office (140 sq ft, exclusive use); rent is $2,400/month for 620 sq ft total. Student loan interest: $3,600 (Navient, 2017–2019). I donated $1,350 to St. Mary's Food Bank (have the receipt) have receipt, and had $1,350 in work expenses. What can I deduct, and should I itemize or take the standard deduction? What forms do I need?
Assistant: I can help — below is a practical breakdown, an estimate of how this will affect your 2023 federal return, and the forms you’ll likely need. I’m not a CPA; consider confirming with tax software or a tax professional (especially if any facts differ from what I’ve assumed).

Key facts I’m using from your message
- Filing status: Head of Household (HOH), federal 2023
- W‑2 wages: $64,800
- 1099 self‑employment (marketing, 2 clients): $15,000
- Interest: $1,450 (Goldman Sachs Marcus) + $320 (TD Ameritrade) = $1,770
- Rent: $2,400/month → $28,800/year on a 620 sq ft rental
- Home office: 140 sq ft, exclusive use (140/620 = 22.58% of home)
- Student loan interest: $3,600 (you wrote 2017–2019 — please confirm whether $3,600 was actually paid in 2023)
- Charitable cash donations: $1,350 (you have receipt)
- “Work expenses” $1,350 — please confirm whether these are expenses of your 1099 self‑employment business (deductible on Schedule C) or unreimbursed employee expenses for W‑2 work (NOT deductible for 2018–2025)

What you can (generally) deduct
- Home office: Yes — because you have 1099 self‑employment income, you can take a home office deduction for the business portion of your rent/utilities if the office is used regularly and exclusively and is your principal place of business.
  - Allocation: 140 / 620 = 22.58%.
  - Rent portion = 22.58% × $28,800 ≈ $6,503. This would be a Schedule C business expense if you use the actual expense method (it’s much larger than the simplified method: 140 sq ft × $5 = $700).
  - You can also include business portion of utilities, renter’s insurance, etc. (if you use actual method).
- Self‑employment business expenses: The $1,350 you listed as work expenses — if these are business expenses for your 1099 marketing work, they are deductible on Schedule C in full.
  - If those are unreimbursed employee expenses for W‑2 employment, they are NOT deductible for 2018–2025.
- Student loan interest: The maximum federal student loan interest deduction is $2,500 (not the full $3,600). Also:
  - The deduction only applies to interest you actually paid in 2023 (so confirm timing).
  - It phases out based on Modified AGI (for single/HOH in 2023 the phaseout starts around $75,000 and ends around $90,000). If your MAGI is below the phaseout start you can take the full $2,500.
- Charitable contributions: $1,350 is deductible, but only if you itemize (on Schedule A). There is no general above‑the‑line charitable deduction for non‑itemizers in 2023.
- Half of your self‑employment tax: deductible as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1 (this reduces AGI).
- Potential QBI (Qualified Business Income) deduction: You may be eligible for a 20% QBI deduction on qualified net self‑employment income (Form 8995). This depends on taxable income and the nature of the business — mention this to your preparer or tax software.

Should you itemize or take the standard deduction?
- 2023 standard deduction for Head of Household: $20,800.
- Your likely itemizable amounts from what you provided:
  - Charitable gifts: $1,350
  - Possibly state & local taxes (SALT) up to $10,000 — but you didn’t list property taxes; you rent so likely your SALT (state income tax withheld) plus any property taxes you pay is unlikely to reach $20,800 by itself.
  - Medical expenses would only be deductible to the extent they exceed 7.5% of AGI (you didn’t list these).
- Conclusion: With the numbers you gave, it’s almost certain the standard deduction ($20,800) will be larger than your itemized total. So you will almost certainly take the standard deduction. The charitable $1,350 gives no extra federal tax benefit unless you have other itemizable amounts that push itemized totals above $20,800.

Quick example estimate (approximate)
- Gross income: 64,800 (W‑2) + 15,000 (1099) + 1,770 (interest) = $81,570
- Subtract business expenses (if $1,350 business expenses + home office actual rent portion ~$6,503) = $7,853 → Net business profit ≈ $7,147
- Adjusted income before SE adjustment: 81,570 − 7,853 = 73,717
- Self‑employment tax (approx): net earnings × 15.3% → roughly $1,009; half (~$505) is an adjustment to income
- AGI before student loan interest ≈ 73,717 − 505 = ~73,212
- Student loan interest deduction: at most $2,500 (if paid in 2023 and you are under the phaseout) — you originally stated $3,600, but only up to $2,500 is allowed and only for interest paid in the tax year.
- Standard deduction (HOH) = $20,800 → likely the best choice vs itemizing with the amounts shown.

Forms you’ll likely need (federal)
- Form 1040 (individual return)
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040) — for adjustments to income (e.g., half of SE tax, possibly student loan interest if deductible)
- Schedule B (Form 1040) — if taxable interest and ordinary dividends exceed $1,500 total (your total interest $1,770 → Schedule B applies)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report your 1099 self‑employment income and business expenses, including home office (actual method)
- Schedule SE — to compute self‑employment tax
- Form 8995 (or 8995‑A) — if claiming the QBI (20%) deduction (many filers use the simplified Form 8995)
- Form 1098‑E — your loan servicer should issue this for student loan interest paid (used to substantiate the student loan interest deduction)
- 1099‑INT(s) and any 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC you received — keep the originals for reporting

State filing
- Illinois residents file IL‑1040 (Illinois uses your federal AGI as the starting point). Illinois has a flat rate (about 4.95% in 2023). You’ll report the same income; there’s no federal‑style standard vs itemized decision for the Illinois tax calculation in the same way.

What I recommend you do next
1. Confirm two items for me:
   - Were the $1,350 “work expenses” business expenses related to your 1099 marketing work (i.e., eligible on Schedule C), or are they unreimbursed employee expenses from W‑2 work? (If the latter, they’re not deductible for 2018–2025.)
   - Is the $3,600 student loan interest amount the amount you actually paid in 2023, or is that a cumulative number for earlier years? (Only interest paid in 2023 is deductible on your 2023 return; you should have a 1098‑E for 2023 if interest was paid.)
2. If the $1,350 work expenses are business expenses, use the actual home office method (allocating rent by square footage) — that will likely give you the largest business deduction.
3. Gather documents: W‑2, all 1099s (NEC/MISC, INT), 1098‑E (student loan interest), receipts for charitable donation, receipts for business expenses, and a record showing square footage and rent paid (for home office).
4. Use tax software or a preparer — they’ll compute SE tax, QBI, and the student loan phaseout precisely. If you didn’t make estimated tax payments during 2023, be prepared that you may owe self‑employment tax + income tax when you file.

If you want, I can:
- Estimate a more detailed federal tax bill if you confirm the two items above and whether you paid any estimated taxes in 2023.
- Draft a checklist email of documents to attach to a preparer (or to collect before you file).
